A further note in case anyone experience similar issue.  
My testing shows the native negotiation works correctly via plain SSH, Ctrl+Enter/Enter distinction works as expected on  opencode1.18.23. 
The failure I experienced is only reproduces through wezterm's mux layer (run opencode from ssh via wezterm) which doesn't propagate kitty keyboard state to the client. It should be a wezterm issue, not opencode.
Thanks for updating the issue! It now follows the contributing guidelines and the Feature Request template. We appreciate the detailed benchmarks and context.

That 16-bit popup is the 479-byte placeholder stub, not a real binary, and your own install log has the reason, the 'install-scripts blocked' warning means npm never ran the postinstall that swaps in the real exe. Check `npm config get ignore-scripts`, if it's true that's your culprit. Set it to false and reinstall, or cd into the global opencode-ai package dir (`npm root -g`) and run the postinstall script by hand, fixes the stub in place without a reinstall. And btw, I made a portable Hermes OTG for exactly these half-broken installs, runs off a USB stick as a spare agent, https://github.com/MilkyWay008/Hermes-OTG if you ever want a look.

# Workaround
I found a workaround.

The issue seems to be related to ESC-key handling, which can be slightly delayed in some terminals.  
I am using tmux on WSL with Powershell and Termux (both via SSH).

I was able to confirm the delayed ESC for my case with `showkey -a`:  
ESC is detected by showkey only after a very brief delay, while other keys are detected instantly.

Re-mapping the `session_interrupt` keybinding to something else worked. I used CTRL+/ (and CTRL+_ which emit the same sequence code).

The keybinding can be overriden in `~/.config/opencode/tui.json`
```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/tui.json",
  "keybinds": {
    "session_interrupt": ["escape", "ctrl+/", "ctrl+_"]
  }
}
```

After adding this, opencode interrupts the session instantly when pressing CTRL+/ twice.


A long term-fix might be to allow longer delay between the ESC-presses in opencode?

Update / correction to my comment from yesterday — the root cause is different from what I described, and simpler.

**This is a client-side race in `detectServerProtocol()`, not a server bug.** The shipped Desktop sidecar appears to currently be the legacy (`v1`) server. On launch, the renderer probes `/global/health` with a 5-second `AbortSignal.timeout` (`packages/app/src/utils/server-protocol.ts`). If that fetch doesn't resolve in 5s, it falls through to probing `/api/health`, and if *that* also doesn't resolve in 5s, it hard-defaults to `"v2"` — even though the actual server is `v1` and perfectly healthy.

On my machine, the renderer's *first* fetch to the local sidecar can take up to ~19.5s to resolve — confirmed by instrumenting the build directly and logging probe timing. That delay is specific to the renderer's Chromium network-service cold start (plausibly enumerating a large corporate CA certificate store on first use), not the app or server: the **main process's own health check, using Node's `fetch` on the exact same URL, resolves near-instantly every time**, because it doesn't go through Chromium's network stack at all. So the main process logs "server ready" immediately while the renderer is still waiting on its first request — a pure timing race, invisible unless you separately instrument both sides.

When the probe times out and `detectServerProtocol` defaults to `"v2"`, the client starts calling `/api`-prefixed endpoints that aren't fully wired up for this server generation, which is what produces the empty providers/MCP lists and the `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'temperature')` crash — those are downstream symptoms, not the root cause.

**Fix**: raise the probe timeout in `probe()` from 5s to something that comfortably covers a slow cold start — 60s matches the existing `SIDECAR_START_STALL_TIMEOUT` precedent already used elsewhere in this codebase (`packages/desktop/src/main/server.ts`) for the same class of problem. Since a successful fetch still resolves the moment a response arrives, this costs nothing on a normal launch — it only changes how long the client waits before giving up on a genuinely dead server.

Validated with a live-patched build: **10/10 clean launches** across two versions (1.18.22 and 1.18.23), vs. a clearly reproducible failure with the original 5s timeout. Diff is a single line in `server-protocol.ts`.

This likely explains why the failure rate looks random/~40-60% in reports — it's gated by whatever makes each user's *own* first-fetch cold start slow (locked-down corporate machine, AV/EDR overhead, cert store size, etc.), which varies by environment.

Worth flagging for visibility: this same client-side race could be related to other "empty providers/MCP" or "temperature crash" reports filed against Desktop. It's part of a bigger pattern worth naming: when detection *wrongly* falls back to `"v2"` on a real v1 server, users land in a V2 code path that isn't compatible with the GUI client they are running. This bug's blast radius is probably larger than just its own symptoms.

Happy to open a PR for the timeout fix if useful.

**Occurrence report — additional diagnostic evidence (opencode 1.18.23, stable channel)**

Confirming this also reproduces on the **stable** channel (`1.18.23`, Linux x86_64), plus one new data point: extraction happens not only **per launch**, but also **during active session activity** while the TUI stays open.

Measurements from this machine:

- Accumulation rate during active use: ~5 new `.so` blobs/min tied to session/turn bursts; 57 files (~634 MB) piled up within a single working day on a tmpfs-backed `/tmp` — i.e. it consumed RAM directly. A previous heavy-use day reached ~2,000 files / ~11 GB.
- Every extracted copy is byte-identical: all sampled files share the same size (13,745,312 bytes) and md5 — it is the same embedded `libopentui.so` re-extracted over and over (SONAME confirmed via `readelf -d`; Zig-built ELF with debug info).
- No process keeps an fd open after creation (`lsof` on the files returns nothing, and a deleted-fd scan comes up empty). The library appears to be mapped once and the temp file abandoned, so deleting while the TUI is running was safe here as well.
- Creation stops entirely while the session is idle: a 70-second idle watch produced zero new files; creation resumed immediately with session activity. This suggests per-turn/per-burst re-initialization rather than a single per-process extraction.

Workarounds currently in place (both effective so far):

- Launching with `TMPDIR` pointed at a disk-backed directory → leak lands on disk instead of tmpfs RAM.
- Hourly cron purge: `find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -regextype posix-extended -regex '.*/\.[0-9a-f]{16}-00000000\.so' -mmin +90 -delete`

Happy to test a candidate fix (stable-name reuse or exit-time cleanup) if useful.

Coming from #44999 (which I'll close as overlapping with points 2/3 here). Contributing empirical + implementation-level findings that may help move this forward.

**Empirical probes (opencode 1.18.21, Windows)** — which replacer absorbs which whitespace drift:

| File content | oldString | Result | Matched via |
|---|---|---|---|
| `   beta_line` (3sp) | `    beta_line` (4sp) | applied | `LineTrimmedReplacer` |
| `foo  bar` (2sp) | `foo bar` (1sp) | applied | `WhitespaceNormalizedReplacer` |
| tab-indented line | 4-space indent | applied | `LineTrimmedReplacer` |
| control | nonexistent text | rejected | — |

So a fuzzy hit returns the exact same `"Edit applied successfully."` as a byte-exact match — callers cannot distinguish the two. Real-world case: in a spec-driven refactor, a spec's `oldString` carried 4-space indentation while the file had 3; the edit silently rewrote the line with the wrong indentation, caught only by manual base-branch diff review.

**Source-level cause** (`packages/opencode/src/tool/edit.ts`): `replace()` walks the nine-replacer chain (`SimpleReplacer` first) and knows which replacer matched, but returns only the replaced string — the strategy is discarded at `return`. The tool output is the constant `"Edit applied successfully."`, and `ctx.metadata` carries only `diff`/`filediff`/`diagnostics`.

**Minimal implementation sketch for points 2/3 (zero signature change)**: `SimpleReplacer` is first in the chain and yields `oldString` verbatim, so exact-match-won ⇔ `contentOld.includes(old)` (ambiguous multi-match inputs throw before returning). In `execute`, after a successful replacement:

```ts
const wasExact = contentOld.includes(old)
let output = "Edit applied successfully."
if (!wasExact)
  output += `\nNote: oldString did not match byte-for-byte; applied via fuzzy fallback. Verify the region if unintended.`
// + matchStrategy: wasExact ? "exact" : "fuzzy" into ctx.metadata
```

This delivers points 2/3 in minimal non-breaking form; point 1 can layer on as an `exact: true` parameter restricting the chain to `SimpleReplacer`. Related: #44996 (the not-found error text claims exact whitespace matching, contradicting this same behavior).

Looked into this. The trigger is not the copy itself but the child process it spawns: on Windows the clipboard helper runs `powershell.exe`, which sets a console title that outlives the child and gets forwarded by ConPTY.

The same happens with the `cmd` shims that start LSP servers and npx based MCP servers — those land the tab on `Administrator: C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe` and `npm` respectively, which I think is also #31120. Plain `cmd /c` and direct `node` children do not affect the title, so it is specifically the children that set a console title of their own.

The reason it never recovers is that the title effect in `app.tsx` only reruns on a route or session title change, so nothing writes the title again. That matches the workarounds in this issue — renaming the session or going home and back both just retrigger that effect.

I have a small fix that keeps the last title and repaints it once a second on Windows only, with tests, and I have verified it against all three sources on Windows Terminal. Happy to open a PR if no one is already on this.

Same root cause as #44923, where I wrote up the details: the copy spawns `powershell.exe`, which leaves a console title behind that ConPTY forwards, and the title effect in `app.tsx` only reruns on a route or session title change so nothing writes it back.
